lead: Dataset augmentation makes more training data without new labels: flip an image, shift a sound, or paraphrase a sentence, and keep the same target. Hyperparameter tuning chooses the settings that gradient descent cannot learn, such as learning rate η, batch size B, weight decay λ and dropout p. Both work against overfitting and wasted compute. You meet them in every image classifier, speech recognizer and text model, from a phone camera app to a bank's fraud model.
prereq: You need: 2.2 for batch size and epochs, 2.4 for optimizer settings, and 2.8 for λ and dropout p.

blocks.text: Parameters are learned by gradient descent: weights and biases. Hyperparameters are set before training: learning rate η, batch size B, weight decay λ, dropout p, and network depth. Their gradient does not exist, so you search on a validation split.

Augmentation grows the training set with label-preserving changes. A horizontal flip keeps a cat a cat. For digits, a 180° rotation turns 6 into 9, and a left-right flip gives a mirrored 6, so flips and rotations of that kind change the label and are wrong for digits. The label must survive, and augmented copies go only into training.

Tuning uses three splits: training, validation, test. Train on training data, compare runs on validation, and touch test once at the end. Keep the same seed and epoch budget for every run. The figure shows 9 runs; the best cell is 0.88 at η = 0.01, B = 128.

Images. Use horizontal flips, random crops with padding, small rotations (about ±10°), colour jitter, and cutout (black out a small square). Avoid vertical flips for upright letters and crops that remove the object.
x̃ = λ x<sub>i</sub> + (1 − λ) x<sub>j</sub>,  ỹ = λ y<sub>i</sub> + (1 − λ) y<sub>j</sub>
blocks.where: x<sub>i</sub>, x<sub>j</sub> are two images; y<sub>i</sub>, y<sub>j</sub> are their one-hot labels; λ ∈ [0, 1] is a mixing weight. This is mixup, an advanced extra.

blocks.text: Audio. Shift the clip a little in time, or add low-level background noise such as fan hum. Keep the spoken word and its label; do not shift the event out of the clip.

Text. Paraphrasing or back-translation (translate to another language and back) adds wording. Use it with care: 'not good' can become 'good' and flip the label. It is risky in sentiment, medical notes and legal text.
Validation and test get one clean, fixed version, such as a centre crop. Augmented copies stay in training.

items: Split data into training, validation and test.
Pick ranges: η on a log scale, say 10<sup>−4</sup> to 10<sup>−1</sup>; B 32 to 512; λ 10<sup>−5</sup> to 10<sup>−2</sup>; p 0 to 0.5.
Fix the seed and epoch budget for all runs.
Run a grid or random search.
Refine coarse-to-fine around the best point.
Score test once with the final model.

blocks.text: Grid search tries every combination. Three η values and three B values make 9 runs; cost multiplies with each added hyperparameter. Random search samples combinations. For the same number of runs it often finds a good configuration because only a few hyperparameters matter. Use a log scale for η and λ, a linear scale for p.
Coarse-to-fine: first try η = 0.1, 0.01, 0.001; if 0.01 wins, try 0.03, 0.01, 0.003.

Schedules. Step decay multiplies η by 0.1 at set epochs. Cosine schedule lowers it smoothly: η<sub>t</sub> = η<sub>min</sub> + ½(η<sub>max</sub> − η<sub>min</sub>)(1 + cos(π t/T)). Here t is the current epoch and T is the total epochs. Tune the schedule and early-stopping patience too.
Bayesian optimization builds a model of validation score against settings and chooses the next run; advanced.

figure.caption: Validation accuracy for the nine-run grid: rows are learning rate 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 and columns are batch size 32, 128, 512. The marked cell, 0.88, is the best run, at learning rate 0.01 and batch size 128.

spec.title: Grid search: rows = learning rate, columns = batch size (32, 128, 512)
spec.aria: A three by three table of validation accuracies, one row per learning rate and one column per batch size, with the highest value marked in the second column of the middle row.

examples.question: You run a 3 × 3 grid: learning rates 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 against batch sizes 32, 128, 512. Validation accuracies are 0.71, 0.76, 0.72; 0.79, 0.88, 0.85; 0.62, 0.70, 0.74. Each run uses 10 epochs and the same split. (a) Which run wins? (b) What accuracy does it reach? (c) What should be the next search step? Use the test set only once.
steps: Write the rows as learning rates and the columns as batch sizes 32, 128, 512.
Row lr = 0.1: maximum is 0.76 at B = 128.
Row lr = 0.01: maximum is 0.88 at B = 128.
Row lr = 0.001: maximum is 0.74 at B = 512.
Compare the row maxima: 0.76, 0.88, 0.74. The largest is 0.88.
The winning run is lr = 0.01, B = 128, validation accuracy 0.88, which is 88%.
Next: finer grid around 0.01, for example lr = 0.03, 0.01, 0.003 with B near 128, same 10 epochs and same seed. After selecting, train the final model and score test once.
examples.answer: The best run is 0.88 validation accuracy, at learning rate 0.01 and batch size 128; next use a finer grid around 0.01 and batch 128, then score the test set once.
examples.check:
scores = {
    0.1: [0.71, 0.76, 0.72],
    0.01: [0.79, 0.88, 0.85],
    0.001: [0.62, 0.70, 0.74]
}
batches = [32, 128, 512]
best_acc = -1.0
best_lr = None
best_b = None
for lr, row in scores.items():
    for b, acc in zip(batches, row):
        if acc > best_acc:
            best_acc = acc
            best_lr = lr
            best_b = b
print(best_acc)
print(best_lr)
print(best_b)

code.code:
scores = {
    0.1: [0.71, 0.76, 0.72],
    0.01: [0.79, 0.88, 0.85],
    0.001: [0.62, 0.70, 0.74]
}
batches = [32, 128, 512]
best_acc, best_lr, best_b = max((acc, lr, b) for lr, row in scores.items() for b, acc in zip(batches, row))
print(f'{best_acc:.2f}')
print(best_lr)
print(best_b)

traps: Tuning on the test set and reporting that score as generalization. Tune on validation, touch test once at the end.
Augmenting validation or test data, or using random crops at test time instead of one fixed centre crop.
Comparing runs that used different epoch budgets or different seeds, so the validation scores are not comparable.
Calling η, λ or p a parameter learned by backpropagation; they are hyperparameters, set before the run.
Using a label-changing augmentation: vertical flip of digits, a crop that removes the object, or back-translation that drops a negation.

quiz.q: What is a hyperparameter? Give three examples.
quiz.a: A setting chosen before training, not learned by gradient descent. Examples: learning rate η, batch size B, weight decay λ, dropout p, network depth.

quiz.q: State the two rules for augmentation.
quiz.a: The label must survive the change. Augmented copies go only into the training set.

quiz.q: Why must augmented copies stay out of validation and test?
quiz.a: Validation and test must estimate performance on clean, real inputs. Random augmentation there adds noise and can inflate or distort the score. Use one fixed version, such as a centre crop.

quiz.q: A grid has η values 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 and B values 32, 128, 512. How many runs? If the best is η = 0.01, B = 128, what finer η values are sensible?
quiz.a: 3 × 3 = 9 runs. A sensible finer grid is η = 0.03, 0.01, 0.003 with B near 128.

quiz.q: Validation accuracies: η = 0.1 gives 0.80, 0.84, 0.82; η = 0.01 gives 0.86, 0.89, 0.87; η = 0.001 gives 0.70, 0.75, 0.78 for B = 32, 128, 512. Which run wins and with what accuracy?
quiz.a: Row maxima are 0.84, 0.89, 0.78. The best is 0.89 at η = 0.01, B = 128.

quiz.q: Why can random search beat grid search with the same number of runs?
quiz.a: Only a few hyperparameters usually matter. A grid spends runs varying irrelevant settings together; random search samples each important dimension more widely and often finds a good configuration in fewer runs.

quiz.q: A team uses random crops on validation and reports 0.90 validation but 0.80 test. Give two likely causes and one fix.
quiz.a: The 0.90 was measured on randomly cropped inputs, so it is not a clean-input estimate and cannot be compared with the 0.80 test score; a second likely cause is repeated tuning on the same validation set (selection bias) or a genuine train/test distribution shift. Fix: one fixed centre crop on validation and test, tune on validation, score test once.

quiz.q: Contrast step decay and a cosine schedule.
quiz.a: Step decay multiplies the learning rate by a fixed factor at set epochs, so it drops in steps. A cosine schedule lowers it smoothly from η<sub>max</sub> to η<sub>min</sub> following a cosine curve over the total epochs.

beyond: Not for the exam. Learned augmentation policies such as AutoAugment and RandAugment search for strong augmentation pipelines instead of hand-picking them. Bayesian optimization and population-based training tune many models in parallel. In production, augmentation and tuning are often automated in the training pipeline, and a small validation budget decides when to stop. Search for RandAugment, Bayesian optimization and learning-rate schedules.
